clue.text: I step and wade, wobbling in such water

definitions.note: used as a description of water, so it stands for the adjective-like compound

indicators.note: wobbling means unsteady, so the letters of the words before it are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone describes stepping unsteadily through water of a certain depth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wobbling' rearranges I, STEP and WADE (and is only a link). The held text lost the opening I, which the letter count needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Water reaching up to your middle is described as being of that depth, the level where you would be wobbling as you wade.

clue.text: Everything to play for in extra golf tournament …

parts.note: a wide is an extra run conceded in cricket when the ball is bowled out of reach
the Open is a major golf championship

explanation.surface: A golf tournament goes to extra holes with the result still in doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a WIDE is one of the 'extras' added to the batting side's score. The ellipsis just links this clue to the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A contest with everything still to play for is one whose outcome is unsettled and could go either way.

clue.text: … that is keeping students occupied

indicators.note: keeping means holding, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students, the UK student body

explanation.surface: Something that keeps students busy, continuing the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: NUS is Britain's National Union of Students; i.e. (id est) is Latin for 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something occupied, like a phone line or toilet, is currently being used by someone.

clue.text: Those people apprehending boy murderers in film

indicators.note: apprehending means catching and holding, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: they means those people
a lad is a boy
killers are murderers

explanation.surface: A group of people catch a boy who turn out to be the murderers in a film plot.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is just 'film': this is the 1955 Ealing comedy about a gang of crooks lodging with an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A classic Ealing comedy film starring Alec Guinness, remade by the Coen brothers in 2004.

clue.text: Asian dish, say, and hot food one ignored? Love to tuck in

parts.note: say introduces an example, abbreviated e.g.

indicators.note: to tuck in means to be pushed inside, so the next piece goes into the shortened word
one ignored means the letter for one, I, is left out of the word

parts.note: a grill, as in a mixed grill, is a hot cooked meal
love is zero in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: Someone eats an Asian dish and hot food, ignoring one portion, and tucks in heartily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one ignored' drops I from GRILL to leave GRLL, and 'to tuck in' puts O (love, nil in tennis) inside it: GROLL.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep-fried pancake parcel of shredded vegetables served in Chinese restaurants, also called a spring roll.

clue.text: Chap dropping line about recent flat stretch?

indicators.note: about means around, so the trimmed name goes round the next piece
dropping means letting go of, so the line letter is removed from the man's name

parts.note: Paul stands for a man, any chap
late can mean recent, as in 'the late news'

explanation.surface: A man gives up a line of work around a recent dull period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes L from PAUL to give PAU, which goes 'about' LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tableland or level upland area, or figuratively a level period with no change.

clue.text: Leads to some mist or gaseous stuff in atmosphere

indicators.note: leads are the front parts, so the opening letters of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: Something hangs in the air like mist or gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leads to' picks the first letters of some, mist, or, gaseous.
explanation.definitionFit: Polluted fog that hangs in the air over cities, a blend of smoke and fog.

clue.text: Bad actor upset a theatrical Irish guru

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: a ham is a bad, overacting actor

indicators.note: theatrical suggests dramatic exaggeration, so the following letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A hammy performer camps up an Irish holy man on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns HAM into MAH; 'theatrical' rearranges IRISH as RISHI.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu sage or spiritual teacher, the title famously held by the Beatles' mentor.

clue.text: Place for the impoverished fish worker?

definitions.meaning: the poor are said to live in the ..., the lowest state of society
one who guts fish, removing the innards, in a fish-processing job

explanation.definitionFit: A roadside drain stands for destitution, and a person who cleans out fish is literally one who removes guts.

clue.text: Nurses mostly leave this or this to work

indicators.note: put to work means set in motion, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement
mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Nurses tend to leave work to one person or another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts LEAVE to LEAV; with THIS, OR, THIS the letters are rearranged by 'to work'.
explanation.definitionFit: Community nurses in Britain who visit homes, especially new mothers and the elderly, to give health advice.

clue.text: Card that will lead to advantage?

definitions.meaning: a two in a pack of playing cards
in tennis the score of forty-all is followed by 'advantage'

explanation.definitionFit: The two of a suit carries this name, and in tennis a tied score of forty-all precedes the call of advantage.

clue.text: Looks amazed about recipe that's peppery-what's peppered things?

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word goes round the letter

parts.note: gapes means stares open-mouthed in amazement
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin recipe meaning 'take'
peppery food is hot

explanation.surface: A cook stares in disbelief at a spicy recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: R for recipe goes inside GAPES. The definition plays on 'peppered', meaning riddled with shot rather than seasoned.
explanation.definitionFit: Small iron balls fired together from a cannon, which spray a target with many hits.

clue.text: Indication of alternative rejected regarding mature herb

parts.note: the word or signals an alternative

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the following pair of words is read backwards

parts.note: on means regarding, as in 'a book on birds'
to age is to mature

explanation.surface: A cook rejects one option in favour of a well-aged herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns 'regarding mature' round as one run, giving EGANO; 'Indication of alternative' is just the word 'or'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mediterranean culinary plant, wild marjoram, used dried in pizza and pasta sauces.

clue.text: Swell, in general, at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters of the word are muddled

explanation.surface: A naval commander's fleet grows as it sails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' rearranges GENERAL. 'Swell' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To swell is to grow bigger, to expand or increase in size.

clue.text: Originally clues in verse had mistakenly to include verse showing optimistic outlook

indicators.note: to include means to take in, so the shuffled letters hold the next piece
mistakenly means in error, so the letters of these words are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A setter writes clues in verse with mistakes, yet keeps a positive attitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Originally' looks like a first-letters signal but is anagram fodder: ORIGINALLY, CLUES, IN, VERSE, HAD are rearranged by 'mistakenly', and 'to include' adds V.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says every misfortune has some good side, which expresses a hopeful attitude to life.

clue.text: Get rid of the lash — time to finish carrying it

parts.note: an era is a period of time

indicators.note: carrying means bearing within, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: to die is to finish, to come to an end
the cat, short for cat-o'-nine-tails, was a whip used for flogging

explanation.surface: A punishment with a whip is abolished: its time has come to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' points back to 'the lash', the whip known as the cat; 'carrying' has the verb for finishing hold it.
explanation.definitionFit: To eliminate something completely, to root it out.

clue.text: Upset one woman after a lot of threatening behaviour

indicators.note: after means that the following pieces come behind the shortened word
a lot of means most of, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: aggro is British slang for aggressive, threatening behaviour
I is the Roman numeral for one
Eve is a woman's name, the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: A woman is distressed after enduring much intimidation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' cuts AGGRO to AGGR. AGGRO is British slang for hostile, threatening behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrieve is to distress or wrong someone, causing resentment.

clue.text: See 14
Measuring scale more suited to early SF writer?

definitions.meaning: a small sliding scale used for precise readings on calipers

definitions.text: more suited to early SF writer?
definitions.meaning: read as Verne plus -ier, more like Jules Verne, a pioneer of science fiction

explanation.definitionFit: A sliding auxiliary scale for fine measurement is named after Pierre Vernier; jokingly it is a comparative of Jules Verne's name.

clue.text: Marine event? Great swimming, thanks

indicators.note: swimming suggests movement in water, so the letters of the word are moved around

parts.note: ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: Someone thanks a great swimmer at a seaside event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimming' rearranges GREAT to REGAT. TA is British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: A series of boat races, an event held on water.

clue.text: Smaller, not at first drawn out

indicators.note: not at first means the opening letter is left off

parts.note: reduced means made smaller

explanation.surface: Something made smaller is not drawn out at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not at first' removes R from REDUCED.
explanation.definitionFit: To educe is to elicit or bring out, so this past form means elicited or extracted.

clue.text: Carmaker to intend line blocking BMW's article

indicators.note: blocking means obstructing from within, so the pieces sit in the middle of the article

parts.note: BMW is German, and der is the German masculine 'the'
to aim is to intend

explanation.surface: A car company plans a production line to block a rival German firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'BMW's' means 'German': DER is a German definite article.
explanation.definitionFit: A German motor manufacturer, founded by Gottlieb Daimler, associated with Mercedes-Benz.

clue.text: Refuse to chase trace of gold — it's superficial dazzle

indicators.note: to chase means to follow behind, so the next word comes after the letter
trace of means just a hint, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: litter is refuse, rubbish

explanation.surface: Junk follows a hint of gold, which is merely shallow sparkle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' is the noun (rubbish), not the verb. LITTER follows G.
explanation.definitionFit: Showy brilliance or glamour that has no real substance.

clue.text: Scottish links run into urban area there

indicators.note: into means entering, so the letter goes inside the word

parts.note: toon is Scots for town, the urban area in Scotland
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A Scottish golf course runs into a nearby town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there' means in Scotland, where TOON is the local word for town.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous Ayrshire golf course, a seaside golf course of the kind called links, which hosts the Open.

clue.text: Snowboarder's aid? Head of board's illuminated without fail, initially

parts.note: the chair heads a board meeting

indicators.note: without means outside, so the word goes round the letter

parts.note: lit means illuminated

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A board's chairman shone, never failing from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here: LIT goes around F, from 'fail, initially'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski lift of seats hung from a moving cable that carries skiers and boarders up the slopes.

clue.text: Australian taking drug in form of a gas

parts.note: Oz is slang for Australia, Australian
on means taking, as in 'on medication'
E is the abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: An Australian on drugs is in a gaseous state.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'on' a drug is to be taking it; E is ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: A form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule, found in the upper atmosphere.

clue.text: Piece for two expected third initially

parts.note: due means expected, as in 'the train is due'

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A two-hander was predicted to come third.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes T from 'third'.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical composition for a pair of performers.

clue.text: Ends sea trips after men recalled approach to travel?

indicators.note: after means the rearranged letters come behind the reversed piece
recalled means called back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: OR stands for Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers or men

indicators.note: trips means stumbles, so the letters of the following words are tripped into a new order

explanation.surface: Sea voyages end after the soldiers are called home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns round the soldiers (other ranks, a military abbreviation), and 'trips' shuffles the first two words into ADSENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Good judgement and awareness of hazards when driving or walking on the roads, a manner of tackling travel.
